content: More than 40,000 individuals sustain eye injuries annually while engaging in sports activities. Sports-related eye injuries are most commonly associated with baseball, basketball, and racquet sports. In the workplace, numerous employees experience job-related eye injuries that necessitate medical intervention. Approximately one-third of these injuries are treated in hospital emergency departments, and over 100 cases result in at least one or more days of missed work. The majority of these injuries are caused by small particles or objects that strike or abrade the eye. Examples include metal slivers, wood chips, dust, and cement fragments, which may be ejected by tools, carried by the wind, or fall from above a worker. Certain objects, such as nails, staples, or slivers of wood or metal, can penetrate the eyeball, leading to permanent vision loss. Larger objects may also impact the eye or face, causing blunt force trauma to the eyeball or the surrounding orbital structures. Chemical burns to one or both eyes are frequently caused by splashes of industrial chemicals or cleaning agents. Thermal burns to the eye are also a recognized hazard. Among welders, their assistants, and nearby workers, ultraviolet (UV) radiation burns—commonly referred to as welder’s flash—routinely damage the eyes and surrounding tissues. In addition to these common eye injuries, certain occupational groups, including healthcare workers, laboratory personnel, janitorial staff, animal handlers, and others, may face an elevated risk of contracting infectious diseases through ocular exposure.
